decision: A member prefix and a feature element, exactly as KerML 8.2.4.1.6 states it. No keyword: this is the plain way a feature becomes a member of a type, and it is the form nearly every feature in a corpus file takes.
notes:
The clause and the Xtext agree exactly.

FOR A PARSER AUTHOR: this contributes no terminal of its own and opens with a nullable reference, so it cannot be recognised at its own first token. Against its sibling TypeFeatureMember the rule is simple — the absence of `member` after the optional visibility indicator selects this one — but note that this production is also shape-identical to NamespaceFeatureMember from clause 8.2.3.4.1, which is likewise MemberPrefix followed by FeatureElement. The two are told apart by context, not by text: NamespaceFeatureMember is reached through NamespaceMember in a namespace body, this one through FeatureMember in a type body. Nothing lexical separates them.

The difference between the two siblings here is in the abstract syntax, not the text: the clause gives this one FeatureMembership and TypeFeatureMember OwningMembership. That belongs to whoever builds the element.

The empty corpus_instances is expected for a production that adds no text of its own.

evidence.note: OwnedFeatureMember is stated there as MemberPrefix followed by FeatureElement
the pilot rule has the same body, MemberPrefix then FeatureElement
